examples.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality with Exponential Functions on Both Sides
examples.worked_solution:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot {5}^{x} & <{7}^{3-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {5}^{x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{3-x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x}) & <\operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{3-x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+x\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <(3-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡7 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡3+x\operatorname{ln}⁡5 & <3\operatorname{ln}⁡7-x\operatorname{ln}⁡7 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡5+x\operatorname{ln}⁡7 & <3\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡5+\operatorname{ln}⁡7) & <3\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x & <\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5+\operatorname{ln}⁡7}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}-{e}^{x-2} & >\frac{4}{5} \\ -{e}^{x-2} & >\frac{3}{5} \\ {e}^{x-2} & <-\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because a power of a positive number is always greater than $0,$ we must have

$$
{e}^{x-2}>0
$$

for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the inequality ${e}^{x-2}<-\frac{3}{5}$ has no solutions.
